DILG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT DILG-NAPOLCOM Center, EDSA cor. Quezon Avenue, West Triangle, Quezon City www.dilg.gov.ph DILG OPINION No. 113 s. 2021 September 13, 2021 MAYOR JOSIE M. BONIFACIO Municipality of Cortes Province of Surigao del Sur Dear Mayor Bonifacio: This refers to your letter dated 02 August 2021 seeking advice relative to your ongoing predicament with the Sangguniang Bayan that began in March 2020. As culled from your Letter, the Sangguniang Bayan (SB) are not amenable to the inclusion of allocation for Job Orders in your Supplemental Budget. Apparently, during last year's budget preparation, funds had been allocated for all Budget Proposals by the Heads of Offices including Job Order requirements. However the SB had slashed such budget on their insistence that these Job Orders are excessive. Ostensibly, certain SB members "have floated the idea that only less than half of the Job Orders would have their contracts renewed in January 2021 without just cause when there is ample budget. " The SB had slashed the budget in half for various units, such as the Office of the Municipal Agriculturist, the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office. The lengthy issue proffered in the subject letter may be encapsulated to the acts of the SB in reducing the budget allocation or slashing of allocated budget for Job Order (JO) personnel in the various offices of herein concerned sanggunian; and its limitation of job orders in various offices. As represented in your letter, majority of the JO personnel had not received remuneration for services rendered since July. As such you are apprehensive that majority of the JOS will have no stipend or salary. The questions herein proffered for this Department's legal opinion are: 1. Is there any merit to these actions undertaken by the SB? and; 2. On what authority and grounds do the SB have to decide how many Job Orders the executive branch needs? Foremost, we note that our regional office has acted upon on the issue concerning the hiring of confidential positions, as such we will no longer touch such issue. Coming now to the subject queries, we deemed it wise to address the foregoing questions in one discussion as they are interrelated. Matino, Mahusay at Maasahan" Trunkline No.: 8876-34-54

At the outset, it may not be amiss to revisit what constitute "job orders" (JOS). The Civil Service Commission (CSC) in its Resolution No. 020790, dated 5 June 2002 described the same, thus: "Section 1. Definitions. The terms hereunder shall be construed, as follows: a. Individual Contract of Services/Job Order- refers to employment described as follows: 1. The contract covers lump sum work or services such as janitorial, security, or consultancy where no employer- employee relationship exists between the individual and the government; 2. The job order covers piece work or intermittent job of short duration not exceeding six months and pay is on a daily basis; 3. The contract of services and job orders are not covered by Civil Service law, rules and regulations, but covered by Commission on Audit (COA) rules; 4. The employees involved in the contract or job order do not enjoy the benefits enjoyed by government employees, such as PERA, ACA and RATA; 5. Services rendered thereunder are not considered as government service." Parenthetically, Section 2 thereof states that 'the employment referred to in Section 1 (a) requires the execution of either a contract of services or memorandum of agreement (MOA) or job order between the government agency concerned and the individual, in accordance with the rules and regulations of the COA. With respect to institutional contracts of services defined in Section 1 (b) a contract of services or a memorandum of agreement must be executed between the hiring government agency and the contracted agency, also subject to the COA rules and regulations. " Further, page 17 of the CSC's A Guide for Local Chief Executives (LCEs) on Public Personnel Administration had succinctly defined job order as the one issued to a person to do piece of work or intermittent job of short duration not exceeding six (6) months paid on a daily basis for local projects authorized by the Sanggunian concerned. Having examined what constitute JOS, attention is again invited to the pertinent provisions of the Local Government Code of 1991 (LGC). Section 77 of the LGC, provides: "Section 77. Responsibility for Human Resources and Development. - The chief executive of every local government unit shall be responsible Page 2 of 4

for human resources and development in his unit and shall take all personnel actions in accordance with the Constitutional provisions on civil service, pertinent laws, and rules and regulations thereon, including such policies, guidelines and standards as the Civil Service Commission may establish: Provided, That the local chief executive may employ emergency or casual employees or laborers paid on a daily wage or piecework basis and hired through job orders for local projects authorized by the sanggunian concerned, without need of approval or attestation by the Civil Service Commission: Provided, further, That the period of employment of emergency or casual laborers as provided in this Section shall not exceed six (6) months. Xxx". (Emphasis ours) Corollarily, Section 22 (c) of the LGC also states: "Section 22. Corporate powers — xxx (c) Unless otherwise provided in this Code, no contract may be entered into by the local chief executive in behalf of the local government unit without prior authorization by the sanggunian concerned. A legible copy of such contract shall be posted at a conspicuous place in the provincial capitol or the city, municipal or barangay hall." (Emphasis ours) As could be gathered from the foregoing provisions, the local chief executive is authorized to hire job order personnel. It is worthwhile to note that the LGC did not limit the number of JOS to be employed in the local government units, nor did it cloth the sanggunian the power to determine how many numbers of JOS in the sanggunian — let alone in the executive branch. Simply put, there is nothing in the LGC that categorically confers authority upon the sanggunian to decide how many job orders there should be in the executive branch. Accordingly, this Department is of the view that the authority of the local chief executive to hire JOS necessarily includes the authority to determine the number of JO personnel in his unit applying the doctrine of necessary implicationsl. Hence, it is the sole authority of the local chief executive to determine the number of JOS in his office. Corollarily, however, the Code requires the approval or authorization from the sanggunian in hiring JO personnel in the office of the executive branch. This authorization is necessary to see to it that the system of check and balance is maintained. Needless to state, sans approval or authorization from the sanggunian, 1 No statute can be enacted that can provide all the details involved in its application. There is always an omission that may not meet a particular situation. What is thought, at the time of enactment, to be an all-embracing legislation may be inadequate to provide for the unfolding events of the future. So- called gaps in the law develop as the law is enforced. One of the rules of statutory construction used to fill in the gap is the doctrine of necessary implication. The doctrine states that what is implied in a statute is as much a part thereof as that which is expressed. Every statute is understood, by implication, to contain all such provisions as may be necessary to effectuate its object and purpose, or to make effective rights, powers, privileges or jurisdiction which it grants, including all such collateral and subsidiary consequences as may be fairly and logically inferred from its terms. Ex necessitate legis. And every statutory grant of power, right or privilege is deemed to include all incidental power, right or privilege. This is so because the greater includes the lesser, expressed in the maxim, in eo plus sit, simper inest et minus." (Emphasis ours) see: Chua vs. Civil Service Commission, 206 SCRA 65, G.R. No. 88979 February 7, 1992 Page 3 of 4

the power of the local chief executives maybe abused. This is the evil sought to be avoided by the Code in requiring the authorization from the SB. As such, this Department submits that the prerogative of hiring JO personnel must not be read as an unqualified authority of the LCE. Since the LCE is vested with a duty being the official responsible for the Human Resources and Development of the LGU, it is our considered view that hiring of JO personnel necessarily includes the authority to determine the number of JO personnel to be hired in order to support the LCE in properly carrying-out the LCE's general supervision and control functions over programs, projects, services, and activities of the LGU. However, this authority must be canalized within the ambit of good governance, administrative necessity, and fiscal adequacy of the LGU so as to ensure efficiency of fund spending and temper any propensity of abuse. Corollary to this is the responsibility to ensure that the hiring of emergency or casual employees or laborers paid on a daily wage or piecework basis and hired through job orders must be anchored from a valid and reasonable grounds such as but not limited to fund availability, actual necessity, among others equally important, reasonable, and legal considerations so as not to prejudice governance, public funds, and public service delivery. This opinion is being rendered without prejudice to any contrary opinion of competent authorities and the courts. We hope to have guided you accordingly. Thank you. ruly yours, BY TH AUTHORITY OF THE SECRETARY: MARLO AN reta for Local Government OUSLG/MLl/LLLS-LRALLD/jam/OUSLG-anor DIR. LILIBETH A. FAMACION, CESO Ill DILG Caraga Bldg., Purok IA Brgy. Boongan, Butuan City Page 4 of 4
